Phosphodiesterase inhibitors such as sildenafil have also shown some benefit in pulmonary arterial hyperten- sion,33,34 and may have a role, particularly in patients who fail to respond to other therapies.1,10 Another alternative may be to use a combination of treatments, such as a pros- tacyclin analogue with an endothelin receptor antagonist, but this suggestion is based on limited evidence and is not yet established.1,6,10 There have been case reports35-37 sug- gesting benefit with imatinib, a platelet-derived growth factor antagonist, but controlled studies are needed. Surgical intervention, and ultimately lung or heart-lung transplantation may be needed in patients who do not re- spond to vasodilator therapy.1,9 Pulmonary hypertension associated with an estab- lished cardiopulmonary disorder is much more com- mon than pulmonary arterial hypertension and the clinical manifestations are dominated by those of the underlying condition. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the commonest respiratory cause, but it may also occur in pa- tients with respiratory distress syndromes, sarcoidosis, or cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis. Pulmonary arterial pres- sure may also be raised in thromboembolic disease, and in patients with impaired left ventricular function, for exam- ple associated with myocardial infarction or mitral valve disease. Management generally involves appropriate treat- ment of the underlying disorder. Inhaled nitric oxide has been used in patients with acute pulmonary hypertension following cardiac surgery or associated with respiratory distress syndrome.38 There have also been reports39 of long-term use in patients with chronic lung disease. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, sometimes also termed persistent fetal circulation, is a form of pulmonary hypertension specifically affecting neo- nates. It can be primary in nature (that is, idiopathic, affect- ing infants with an anatomically normal heart and no pul- monary disease) or secondary, being associated with a number of cardiopulmonary conditions including congen- ital heart disease, diaphragmatic hernia, meconium aspira- tion, respiratory distress syndrome, or sepsis. The pulmo- nary hypertension and altered vasoreactivity lead to a right-to-left shunting of blood across the patent ductus ar- teriosus or foramen ovale and this often results in critical hypoxaemia. Management generally involves high-frequency oscillat- ory ventilation (to achieve optimal lung inflation) and, if necessary, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
